title: As a developer, the reviewer catches real bugs in my PR — logic errors, race conditions, broken edge cases — not just style nits
As an engineering lead, the reviewer keeps noise low — few false positives, deduplicated comments, severity labels — so my team doesn't tune it out
As a developer, I can push back on a bad review comment and the reviewer learns — it stops repeating the same rejected feedback
As a security engineer, reviews flag security problems in the diff — injection risks, leaked secrets, insecure patterns — alongside functional bugs
As a developer, review comments reflect the whole repository — call sites, related modules, existing conventions — not just the changed hunks
As an engineering lead, the reviewer understands changes that span multiple repositories or a large monorepo and reviews them coherently
As an AI-native user, the reviewer builds a persistent memory of my team's conventions and past review decisions and applies it to future PRs
As a developer, the reviewer installs as a GitHub/GitLab app and posts reviews as native inline comments on my pull requests within minutes
As a developer, every PR gets an auto-generated summary and change walkthrough so human reviewers orient fast
As a developer, review comments include committable suggested diffs I can apply with one click
As a developer, pushing new commits triggers an incremental re-review that tracks what was fixed instead of repeating old comments
As an engineering lead, I configure the reviewer with a versioned config file in my repo — path filters, per-path instructions, review profiles
As an engineering lead, I encode my team's own review guidelines — natural-language rules, AST patterns, or linked style guides — and the reviewer enforces them
As an engineering lead, I roll out org-level review defaults across hundreds of repos and manage exceptions centrally
As a developer, I reply to the reviewer in the PR thread to ask questions, get explanations, or issue commands — and it answers in context
As a developer, I control when reviews run — skip drafts, trigger on demand, filter by branch or label — so the bot shows up only when wanted
As a developer, I turn a review finding into an applied fix — a committed patch or an agent-generated follow-up — without leaving the PR
As an AI-native user, I define custom agentic pre-merge checks in plain language — 'docs updated', 'tests cover new paths' — that run on every PR
As an AI-native user, review findings hand off cleanly to my coding agent — copyable fix prompts or direct integration with Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex
As an AI-native user, the reviewer holds the line on AI-generated PRs — it verifies agent-authored code at a volume no human team could review
As an engineering lead, the reviewer can gate merges — a required status check or blocking review that enforces resolution of critical findings
As an engineering lead, I see dashboards of findings, acceptance rates, and review coverage across my org
As a developer, I get the same review inside my IDE before I push, catching issues while the code is still in my editor
As a developer, I run reviews from a CLI against local diffs or in CI scripts, with machine-readable output my tooling can consume
